title: Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative
hookLine: the Appreciative, who rewards the smallest good

lines: A THORNY BRANCH ON THE ROAD.
cards: You held a door. You wiped the counter someone else left sticky. You moved the scooter off the sidewalk so the next person with a stroller wouldn't have to.
Nobody saw. Nobody said thanks. Easy to file under: didn't count.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told of a man walking down a road who found a thorny branch lying across it. He moved it out of the way, so it wouldn't hurt anyone. That's the whole deed.
And the hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says God thanked him for it, and forgave him. God thanked him. For a branch.

teach.b: Ash-Shakur comes from shukr, the word for thanks from the very start of the path. A person with shukr is grateful. But God doesn't need anything from us, so what does it mean for him to be shakur?
Scholars explain it as appreciation: he notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. A branch moved, a whole life forgiven. That's the scale.
The Qur'an puts it in two short lines near its end.
In Pickthall's translation: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then." In the Arabic it's a dharrah, a speck, some say the tiniest ant. Nothing is too small to be seen, and answered.
And the Prophet backed it up in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: don't look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. A smile is on the list.
Now look back at this week, because every name has pointed here. Al-Fattah opened. Al-'Alim knew what the heart hides.
As-Sami' heard the woman in Medina. Al-Latif worked too finely to see. Al-Halim held back.
Al-Wadud loved, and showed it. And Ash-Shakur notices the smallest thing you did, and doesn't let it disappear.
Seven days, eight names, one picture running through them: in the Qur'an's telling, nothing a person does is too small, too quiet, or too hidden to count.

how: Many Muslims take the hadith of the thorny branch literally and clear obstacles from paths and roads, and the Prophet counted removing harm from the road as a branch of faith.

o: the One who notices small good and repays it richly
the One who needs and expects people's thanks
the One who rewards only the biggest good deeds

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: moved off the road, and thanked
a good deed not to look down on

s: the hadith says God thanked the man who moved a branch
God thanked him and forgave him, in Sahih al-Bukhari.
shakur means God needs our thanks
it means God appreciates: he notices small good and rewards it beyond its size.
a smile counts as a good deed in the hadith
don't look down on any good, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face.

games.q: you're walking down a road and there's a thorny branch lying across it. nobody's watching. what do you do?
o: step over it. not your branch.
move it out of the way.
tell someone else to move it.
games.why: the man in the hadith moved it, and God thanked him and forgave him. the smallest deed, answered at full size.

practice: Go back over today and find the smallest kind thing anyone did for you: the barista who remembered your name, the coworker who refilled the printer, the kid who put their plate in the sink without being asked.
Choose one, and picture thanking them, naming the small thing so they know it was seen. If you pray, you can thank God for it too.

wordCard.voice: Ash-Shakur. The Appreciative: the One who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Appreciative. from shukr, thanks: here, the One who rewards small good richly.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing small is lost. Not even a branch moved off a road. Day two hundred fifty-two, and a week of names, done.

sources.q: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then
